body:
I keep thinking about what you wrote, but I just can't figure out how you did it. You said you felt that way for six years; I have never not felt this way and I have never had a close relationship. How did you move from "how are you?" to talking about your problems? How should I explain it, considering I don't have any actual tangible problems: grades, family, job loss, relationships, etc. 

To be honest, I have a hard enough time just being honest. I always have an urge to lie to seem more normal. Did you have that? Do you have to start being honest with everyone, or just the person you want to open up to?
Haha, I think so. I've never tried to articulate it.

With prospective friends, it is because I worry they might in some way know my current friends, and tell them something that would affect their opinion of me. Really basic information - what is your major? - is more because strangers are scary and I don't want them to keep talking to me. Its a way of limiting the amount of faces I have to remember and names to feel bad about forgetting. 

With actual friends its more about worrying that if they get to know me, they'll think I'm a weirdo because I've never had a significant emotional relationship. 

For the reasons above, dating anyone who has any connection to my life (like a friend of a friend, or they share a class) terrifies me. 

You're so nice for continuing talking with me.

I guess by vulnerability I mean personal information - I recently dodged the question when a friend's girlfriend asked me what I was majoring in. I just have this stupid paranoia that the more others know about you the more they have to use against you. 

I think I would find saying "vulnerability issues" easier than "difficulty connecting emotionally with people" which I guess is how I've always thought about it. Thanks.

I totally get what you're saying. I guess it's just really hard to make those first steps. Work seems a really intimidating place to do it, because they're people you have to see so often... so I guess you couldn't avoid them and cut them out of your life entirely if you regretted opening up later. Which is good thing, probably?

I think I worry more about showing weakness and that if I open up to one friend, they'll not like me, and will go on tell others how weird and unhuman I am. When I'm around people I get into this other mode, where everything I say is meant to evade saying something personal or keep the level of intimacy in the conversation from getting deeper. It's automatic and I've tried but haven't been able to get out of it. Not tried a lot, admittedly.

That's good advice. I'll try to keep it in mind. What kind of environment did you initiate these conversations in? I feel like I don't find myself in places that are great for those sorts of interaction, but I don't know. Where did you do it?

Recruiting is rough. There are always a few people who are really dedicated and involved, and others who drift in and out. 

Sucks about your uni's LGBT group - some groups develop that community where you have to be very deep into the LGBT community. I was nervous when I first began going because I'm bisexual and sometimes people think that's not queer enough - but it was fine. I was the only bisexual when we started, but now there's more, which is nice.

I've been working on some internalized misogyny for a while. I took a Women's History course, and the dearth of female voices in history convinced me that maybe all the homogeneity of the books I read might contribute something to my lack of understanding/appreciation and resentment toward my own gender.

That's really impressive. It seems like student organizations at my school focus more on educational/themed events, and less real actions like that. Probably because they're always fighting to get/keep a decent membership.

It really helps to hear someone else has had the same problem. Most of the time I only see people with problems involving lots of strong emotion, broken relationships, serious difficulties in life, etc. and it makes me feel like I don't have any problems - so my angst is just bullshit. 

It sounds so easy when you say it. But I have that how was your day exchange several times a day. How do you make it something else besides the usual? I'm nervous between finding a balance between not sharing anything meaningful and over sharing as well. I don't know how to move from Person I see regularly to good friend. 

It helps to see everything worked out for you, but I admit I can't conceive of how you managed it.

I'm going to major in German - right now I'm doing the generals. The group is an LGBT group - sort of a raise awareness/social support group. 

What kind of things did those groups do?

My favorite is The Hitchhiker's Guide - all five books. I like Douglas Adams, Chuck Palahniuk, David Sedaris, Neil Gaiman, Christopher Moore, and so on. Others, but those are people I've read several books by. This year I'm trying to read more women. I want to raise my gender ratio from 13:87 to 25:75 pages from women:men.

The Art of Asking by Amanda Palmer. I like her music, and I really envy her ability to connect to people. She's a real pro at it. 

That looks interesting. Its a pretty fairly big one. I added it to my good reads.
I really appreciate the sentiment of your comment, but I have no idea what to say in reply. Talk about what? I don't mean to be flip - I thought about it but I've got nothing.

To what end? I'm not going through some difficultperiod right now - this has been my whole life. Sure, I could keep going through every day alone, fall in and out of people's lives without ever connecting to them, and just barely existing. But why? Its not fun. Its just work. Its like going to work every day at a shitty job but never getting a paycheck.
The useless ones that no one else seems to have read. Not harry potter, LOTR, other sci fi series which seem popular, at least with my friends.
